titre: The Book That Made an Eggshell an Argument
accroche: Rachel Carson publishes a book on pesticides in 1962. Her most effective argument comes down to the thickness of a shell
contenu_vulgarise:
DDT emerges from World War II with a halo. It protected troops from typhus and malaria, it is cheap, it kills just about every insect, and it seems harmless to humans at the doses used. It is spread widely on crops, forests and residential neighborhoods.

In 1962, the marine biologist Rachel Carson publishes *Silent Spring*. The title announces a spring without birdsong.

## The Argument That Landed

The book brings together many elements, but one is more effective than the rest, because it is measurable.

DDT breaks down slowly and dissolves in fat. It is therefore not eliminated: it accumulates in the tissues of the organisms that ingest it. And at each level of the food chain, a predator eats many prey, and so concentrates what each of them had accumulated.

At the top of that chain, birds of prey receive doses out of all proportion to those that were sprayed.

The effect is not a massive, visible die-off. It affects the formation of eggshells, which thin to the point of breaking under the weight of the bird incubating them. The populations do not die: they stop renewing themselves.

It is a formidable argument because it is verifiable. You can measure the thickness of a shell, and compare it with that of museum collections assembled before the war.

## What the Book Set Off

The chemical industry responded with a campaign aimed at the author as much as at the content. Carson, who had cancer, died less than two years after publication.

The book nonetheless prompted a presidential commission, then the ban on DDT in the United States in 1972. It is also credited with a share in the birth of the modern environmental movement and of the US Environmental Protection Agency.

## What the Case Leaves Open

A debate persists over the consequences of the ban in countries where malaria kills, and it cannot be settled in a sentence.

Two remarks are worth holding together. Carson did not call for a ban, but for an end to massive, indiscriminate spraying; she wrote that blind use would produce resistant insects, which has proved true. And the use of DDT as indoor spraying against malaria has never been universally prohibited; the World Health Organization still recommends it in certain contexts.

What the book durably established is therefore not a ban. It is a notion: a substance can be harmless at the dose at which it is sprayed, and dangerous at the dose at which it ends up concentrated.

repere.texte: Carson popularizes the mechanism by which DDT thins the eggshells of birds of prey until they break. The book appears on September 27, 1962; DDT is banned in the United States in 1972.
repere.source: Natural Resources Defense Council, “The Story of Silent Spring”

carte.punch: A substance can be harmless at the dose sprayed, and dangerous at the dose where it concentrates.
carte.idee: DDT is not eliminated: it accumulates in fat, and concentrates at each level of the food chain. In birds of prey, it thins eggshells. The populations do not die; they stop renewing themselves.
carte.source_courte: NRDC, The Story of Silent Spring

quiz.question: Why were birds of prey the most affected by DDT?
choix: Because they nest in the areas where the product was sprayed first
Because their metabolism breaks down pesticides more slowly than other birds
Because they live longer and so accumulate more over the years
Because at the top of the food chain, they concentrate what their prey have accumulated
quiz.explication: DDT dissolves in fat and is not eliminated. Since each predator eats many prey, the dose multiplies at each level: at the top, it is out of all proportion to the one sprayed. The effect does not kill adults; it thins eggshells until they break under the incubating parent.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to the card, why was DDT praised when it emerged from World War II?
choix: It had protected troops from typhus and malaria, was cheap and killed almost every insect
It had allowed crop yields to double in a single season
It was the first pesticide to be fully biodegradable within hours
It had been invented specifically to protect bird populations
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text recalls that DDT came out of the war with a halo: it had protected troops from typhus and malaria, it was cheap, it killed just about every insect, and it seemed harmless to humans at the doses used.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to the card, what did Rachel Carson actually ask for in Silent Spring?
choix: A total, immediate ban on all use of DDT worldwide
An end to massive, indiscriminate spraying, not a total ban
Replacing DDT with a costlier but biodegradable pesticide
The creation of an international pesticide control agency
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text specifies that Carson did not call for a ban, but for an end to massive, indiscriminate spraying, anticipating that blind use would produce resistant insects, which has proved true.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the card say about the current use of DDT against malaria?
choix: It has been universally prohibited in every country since 1972
It was never used against malaria, only in agriculture
The World Health Organization still recommends it in certain contexts
Its use has been replaced everywhere by insecticide-treated bed nets
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The card specifies that the use of DDT as indoor spraying against malaria has never been universally prohibited, with the World Health Organization still recommending it in certain contexts.
